title: Rust Quiz
description: Review the 12 starter lessons. The questions name the example to revisit. Take your time, use the lessons, and read the reason after each answer.

questions.question: println! prints text and starts a new line. main is the program entry point. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: main starts the program. println! writes the string and adds a newline. println! has an exclamation mark because it is a macro.

questions.question: let creates a name for a value. Values cannot be changed unless you ask for mut. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: let stores 3 under pencils. The {} slot receives the sum 5. A plain let binding cannot be assigned a new value.

questions.question: mut means this binding may change. It makes the choice to change data clear. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: mut permits the change. The += line stores 5 back into score. Use mut only when the value needs to change.

questions.question: if can produce a value. Both branches here return text of the same type. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The true condition chooses Pass as the value stored in message. Both branches used as a value must have matching types.

questions.question: 1..=3 includes both ends. A for loop visits each number in the range. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The ..= range includes 3. Three loop passes print 1, 2 and 3. 1..3 stops before 3; ..= includes the end.

questions.question: A Vec stores values in order. push adds a value at the end. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: vec! creates the vector. push adds 8; {:?} requests a list-style display. The vector must be mutable to push a new item.

questions.code:
fn twice(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 }
fn main() { println!("{}", twice(4)); }
questions.question: The last expression can be a function result. It has no trailing semicolon. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The input n becomes 4. Without a trailing semicolon, n * 2 is returned. A semicolon after n * 2 turns it into a statement with no returned number.

questions.question: A String owns its text. Assigning it to another variable moves that ownership. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: Assigning first to second moves ownership of the String. second is now its usable owner. Do not use a String binding after its value has moved.

questions.question: A reference borrows a value. It lets code read the value while its owner keeps it. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: &name creates a shared reference. It borrows without moving the text, so both borrowed and name can read Asha. A reference must not outlive the value it points to.

questions.question: Option holds Some(value) or None. unwrap_or gives a fallback for None. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: score is None. unwrap_or returns the fallback 0 instead of reading a missing number. unwrap can panic on None; check it or use a fallback.

questions.question: Result holds Ok for success or Err for failure. Parsing text can fail. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: parse::<i32>() cannot read cat as an integer. match therefore uses the Err branch. Do not assume every text value is a valid number.

questions.question: A struct describes named fields. Each Book value can hold its own title. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The struct literal stores owned text in title. The dot reads that field. Supply every required field when making a struct.
